questions.title: Composition of the midbrain tectum
questions.question: The tectum is formed of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The medial and lateral geniculate bodies are thalamic nuclei (relaying auditory and visual information respectively), not components of the midbrain tectum.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei sit at the pontomedullary junction, not in the midbrain tectum.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The superior and inferior salivatory nuclei are pontine and medullary parasympathetic nuclei, unrelated to the tectum.
explanations.D: Correct. The tectum, the roof (dorsal part) of the midbrain, is formed by the corpora quadrigemina: two superior colliculi, which mediate visual reflexes, and two inferior colliculi, which relay auditory information — four colliculi in total. This composition distinguishes the tectum from the tegmentum and crus cerebri, the other two midbrain subdivisions. In short: identify the tectum as being built from four colliculi (two superior, two inferior), not geniculate bodies, salivatory nuclei or cochlear nuclei.

questions.learning_objective: State that the midbrain tectum is formed of the four colliculi (corpora quadrigemina), not geniculate bodies, cochlear nuclei or salivatory nuclei.

questions.title: Internal jugular vein relation to the middle ear
questions.question: The internal jugular vein is related to:

explanations.A: Correct. The jugular bulb, the dilated superior end of the internal jugular vein, sits within the jugular fossa of the temporal bone immediately below the floor of the middle ear (tympanic cavity), separated from it only by a thin, sometimes dehiscent, bony plate. This close relationship explains why a high-riding or dehiscent jugular bulb can present with pulsatile tinnitus or be visible as a bluish mass behind the tympanic membrane. In short: identify the internal jugular vein (via its jugular bulb) as related to the floor, not the roof or walls, of the middle ear.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The roof of the middle ear (tegmen tympani) is related to the middle cranial fossa and temporal lobe of the brain, not the internal jugular vein.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The posterior wall of the middle ear is related to the mastoid antrum and the facial nerve canal, not the internal jugular vein.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The anterior wall of the middle ear is related to the carotid canal (internal carotid artery), not the internal jugular vein.

questions.subtopic: Internal jugular vein and the floor of the middle ear
questions.learning_objective: State that the internal jugular vein (via the jugular bulb) is related to the floor of the middle ear, not its roof, posterior or anterior wall.

questions.title: Mechanism of antagonist relaxation in the stretch reflex
questions.question: In the stretch reflex, relaxation of antagonist muscles is due to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Presynaptic inhibition modulates the strength of afferent input generally (e.g. in pain gating), but it is not the mechanism that specifically relaxes the antagonist muscle during a stretch reflex.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Antidromic conduction (an action potential travelling backward along an axon) is not part of the normal stretch reflex circuit.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ia fiber stimulation is the afferent (sensory) limb of the stretch reflex arising from the muscle spindle, but by itself it does not explain why the antagonist relaxes — that requires the specific circuit described by reciprocal innervation.
explanations.D: Correct. In reciprocal innervation, the same Ia afferent that excites the agonist's alpha motor neurons monosynaptically also excites an inhibitory interneuron in the spinal cord, which in turn inhibits the antagonist muscle's motor neurons (disynaptically). This coordinated excitation of the agonist with inhibition of the antagonist allows the stretched muscle to contract while its opposing muscle relaxes, rather than the two working against each other. In short: identify reciprocal innervation as the spinal circuit responsible for antagonist relaxation during the stretch reflex.

questions.subtopic: Reciprocal innervation in the stretch reflex
questions.learning_objective: State that antagonist muscle relaxation during the stretch reflex is produced by reciprocal innervation (Ia afferent collaterals inhibiting antagonist motor neurons via an interneuron).

questions.title: Thalamic nucleus in emotion and memory processing
questions.question: Which of the following thalamic nuclei plays a role in processing of emotions and memory:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The ventral anterior nucleus is part of the motor thalamus, relaying basal ganglia and cerebellar output to the premotor and prefrontal cortex, not emotion/memory circuitry.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The intralaminar nuclei contribute to cortical arousal (as part of the reticular activating system) and to the slow, diffuse pathway for pain, not specifically to emotion and memory.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The pulvinar is chiefly involved in visual association and multimodal sensory integration, not the emotion/memory circuit.
explanations.D: Correct. The anterior nucleus of the thalamus is a key relay of the Papez circuit — hippocampus, via the fornix, to the mammillary bodies, via the mammillothalamic tract to the anterior thalamic nucleus, to the cingulate gyrus, and back to the hippocampus — the classical anatomical substrate for processing emotion and memory. In short: identify the anterior thalamic nucleus, not the ventral anterior, intralaminar or pulvinar nuclei, as the thalamic component of the Papez (emotion/memory) circuit.

questions.subtopic: Anterior nucleus and the Papez circuit
questions.learning_objective: Identify the anterior nucleus of the thalamus as the thalamic relay of the Papez circuit for emotion and memory processing.

questions.title: Composition of the crista ampullaris cupula
questions.question: Which component of the crista ampullaris is formed of gelatinous layer of proteoglycans?

explanations.A: Correct. The cupula is a dome-shaped, gelatinous mass composed largely of proteoglycans that caps each crista ampullaris and embeds the stereocilia and kinocilium of the underlying hair cells. Angular acceleration of the head drives endolymph flow within the semicircular duct, which deflects the cupula and bends the embedded cilia, generating a receptor potential in the hair cells. In short: identify the cupula, not the tectorial membrane, phalangeal cells or stereocilia themselves, as the gelatinous proteoglycan-rich structure of the crista ampullaris.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The tectorial membrane is a gelatinous structure of the cochlea (organ of Corti), not of the vestibular crista ampullaris.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Phalangeal (supporting) cells are cellular elements that structurally support hair cells, not a gelatinous extracellular matrix.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Stereocilia are the hair cell's own actin-filled sensory processes, embedded within the cupula, not the gelatinous matrix itself.

questions.learning_objective: State that the cupula, a gelatinous proteoglycan mass, forms the structure of the crista ampullaris that embeds the hair cells' stereocilia and kinocilium.

questions.title: Origin of the superior cerebellar artery
questions.question: Superior cerebellar artery arises from:

explanations.A: Correct. The superior cerebellar artery arises from the basilar artery near its terminal bifurcation, just below the origin of the posterior cerebral artery, and it supplies the superior surface of the cerebellum along with part of the midbrain. In short: identify the basilar artery, not the vertebral artery, the circle of Willis as a whole, or the pontine branches, as the parent vessel of the superior cerebellar artery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The vertebral artery gives rise to the posterior inferior cerebellar artery and the anterior/posterior spinal arteries, not the superior cerebellar artery.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The circle of Willis is an anastomotic ring of vessels, not itself a parent artery of origin for a named branch such as the superior cerebellar artery.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pontine (paramedian and circumferential) branches are themselves branches of the basilar artery supplying the pons; they are not the parent vessel of the superior cerebellar artery.

questions.learning_objective: State that the superior cerebellar artery arises from the basilar artery, near its terminal bifurcation.

questions.title: Recognizing the caudate and putamen as basal ganglia nuclei
questions.question: Which of the following is one of basal ganglia nuclei?

explanations.A: Correct. The caudate nucleus and putamen together form the corpus striatum (neostriatum), a core component of the basal ganglia alongside the globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus and substantia nigra. In short: identify the caudate and putamen, not the mammillary bodies, gracile/cuneate nuclei or inferior olive, as genuine basal ganglia nuclei.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The mammillary bodies are hypothalamic structures forming part of the Papez circuit, not basal ganglia components.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The gracile and cuneate nuclei are medullary relay nuclei of the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway, not basal ganglia components.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The inferior olivary nucleus is a medullary nucleus that supplies climbing fibers to the cerebellum, not a basal ganglia structure.

questions.subtopic: Caudate and putamen as basal ganglia nuclei
questions.learning_objective: Recognize the caudate nucleus and putamen as genuine basal ganglia nuclei, distinguishing them from mammillary bodies, gracile/cuneate nuclei and the inferior olive.

questions.title: Sulcus dividing the frontal and parietal lobes
questions.question: The sulcus separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe is

explanations.A: Correct. The central sulcus (of Rolando) runs obliquely from the superomedial border of the hemisphere down toward the lateral sulcus, separating the precentral gyrus (frontal lobe, primary motor cortex) from the postcentral gyrus (parietal lobe, primary somatosensory cortex) — the recognized anatomical boundary between the frontal and parietal lobes. In short: identify the central sulcus, not the lunate, cingulate or transverse sulcus, as the frontal-parietal boundary.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lunate sulcus is an occipital lobe landmark near the primary visual cortex, unrelated to the frontal-parietal boundary.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cingulate sulcus lies on the medial surface, separating the cingulate gyrus from the medial frontal and parietal cortex above it, but it does not itself mark the frontal-parietal boundary on the lateral surface.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The transverse sulcus is not the standard landmark separating the frontal and parietal lobes.

questions.learning_objective: State that the central sulcus separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe.

questions.title: Principal refractive surface of the resting eye
questions.question: Which of the following provides about 2/3 the refractive power of the resting eye?

explanations.A: Correct. Of the resting eye's total refractive power of roughly 59-60 diopters, the anterior corneal surface alone contributes about 40-43 diopters — around two-thirds of the total — because it is where the greatest change in refractive index occurs, from air (1.00) to the cornea (about 1.376). The crystalline lens contributes only the remaining third, and unlike the fixed corneal power, its contribution is the part adjusted during accommodation. In short: identify the anterior corneal surface as the source of about two-thirds of the resting eye's refractive power.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The posterior lens surface contributes comparatively little refractive power, since the refractive index change there (lens to vitreous) is much smaller than at the air-cornea interface.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The posterior corneal surface (cornea to aqueous humor) contributes far less power than the anterior surface, since both media have similar refractive indices.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The anterior lens surface contributes only part of the lens's own one-third share of total refractive power, not the two-thirds attributed to the cornea.

questions.learning_objective: State that the anterior surface of the cornea provides about two-thirds of the resting eye's total refractive power.

questions.title: Composition of the tectorial membrane
questions.question: Which component of the scala media is formed of gelatinous mass with collagen fibrils?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Stereocilia are actin-filled cellular processes of the hair cells themselves, not a gelatinous extracellular matrix.
explanations.B: Correct. The tectorial membrane is a gelatinous, largely acellular structure made of collagen fibrils embedded in a glycoprotein matrix, overlying the organ of Corti within the scala media. Vibration of the basilar membrane creates a shearing force between it and the tectorial membrane, bending the stereocilia of the outer hair cells embedded within it and generating a receptor potential. In short: identify the tectorial membrane as the gelatinous, collagen-fibril-containing structure of the scala media, not the stereocilia, kinocilium or pillar cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mature mammalian outer hair cells lose their functional kinocilium; in any case a kinocilium is a cellular structure, not a gelatinous mass.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pillar (rod) cells are cellular structural elements of the organ of Corti that form the tunnel of Corti, not a gelatinous mass.

questions.learning_objective: State that the tectorial membrane, a gelatinous mass of collagen fibrils, is the structure of the scala media overlying the organ of Corti.

questions.title: Cortical location of lower limb motor control
questions.question: The area responsible to motor control of the lower limb muscles.

options.A: Located in the upper part of the pre central gyrus.
options.C: Located in the upper part of the post central gyrus.

explanations.A: Correct. Per the motor homunculus, the lower limb is represented at the uppermost part of the precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex, area 4) on the lateral surface of the hemisphere, with the leg and foot occupying the vertex region before the representation continues onto the medial surface. In short: identify the upper precentral gyrus as the classically taught seat of lower-limb motor control.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The medial frontal gyrus is not a standard motor homunculus landmark for the lower limb.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The postcentral gyrus is primary somatosensory cortex, not motor cortex, so it does not control lower-limb muscles.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the single best answer here. The paracentral lobule does carry the medial continuation of the leg/foot motor and sensory strips, but the primary and most commonly tested seat of lower-limb motor control on the lateral cortical surface is the upper part of the precentral gyrus, which this question credits.

questions.subtopic: Lower-limb motor representation in the precentral gyrus
questions.learning_objective: State that lower-limb motor control is located in the upper part of the precentral gyrus, per the motor homunculus.

questions.title: Drainage of the transverse cervical vein
questions.question: The transverse cervical vein drains into ONE of the following:

explanations.A: Correct. The transverse cervical vein, accompanying the transverse cervical artery through the posterior triangle of the neck, typically drains into the external jugular vein (sometimes joining it as a common trunk with the suprascapular vein) before the external jugular vein continues on to join the subclavian vein. In short: identify the external jugular vein, not the internal jugular or subclavian vein, as the direct drainage site of the transverse cervical vein.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The suprascapular vein is a companion vessel that may join the transverse cervical vein en route, rather than being the transverse cervical vein's own destination.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The internal jugular vein drains deeper structures of the head and neck (via the facial, lingual and pharyngeal veins, among others), not the posterior triangle's transverse cervical vein.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The subclavian vein is a more distal confluence point, receiving the external jugular vein, rather than the direct drainage site of the transverse cervical vein itself.

questions.learning_objective: State that the transverse cervical vein drains into the external jugular vein.

questions.title: Defining feature of spinal shock
questions.question: In humans, spinal shock is characterized by:

explanations.A: Correct. Spinal shock is the acute, transient state immediately following severe spinal cord injury or transection, characterized by a complete loss (areflexia) of all reflex activity below the level of the lesion, together with flaccid paralysis and hypotonia, resulting from the sudden withdrawal of descending facilitatory input to spinal neurons. In short: identify loss of spinal reflexes, not hyperreflexia, hypertonia or spastic paralysis, as the defining acute feature of spinal shock.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hyperreflexia is a chronic, later finding that emerges only after spinal shock has resolved (days to weeks later), once the isolated cord below the lesion becomes hyperexcitable — the opposite of the acute areflexic state.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hypertonia likewise develops only after spinal shock resolves; the acute phase itself is hypotonic.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Spastic paralysis is the chronic sequela following resolution of spinal shock, whereas the acute spinal shock state itself is flaccid, not spastic.

questions.learning_objective: State that spinal shock is characterized acutely by loss of spinal reflexes below the level of the lesion, distinct from the chronic hyperreflexia/spasticity that follow once it resolves.

questions.title: A true statement about cerebellar function
questions.question: Which of the following is TRUE concerning the cerebellum?

options.A: Damping of movement is a function of the cerebrocerebellum.
options.B: Its function is purely motor control at a subconscious level.
options.C: The spinocerebellum shares in planning of movement.
options.D: It controls muscles of the opposite side of the body.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Damping of movement (preventing overshoot and oscillation) is attributed to the spinocerebellum, which uses ongoing peripheral feedback to smooth movement, not to the cerebrocerebellum.
explanations.B: Correct. Classic physiology teaching holds that the cerebellum's role lies purely within the motor domain — coordinating, timing and correcting movement by comparing intended with actual performance — and that it operates entirely below the level of conscious awareness, without itself initiating movement or entering conscious perception. In short: identify the cerebellum's function as purely motor and subconscious, unlike the other (incorrect) statements about its specific lobar roles or laterality.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Planning of complex voluntary movement, via its connections with the motor and premotor cortex, is attributed to the cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres), not the spinocerebellum.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The cerebellum acts almost entirely on the ipsilateral side of the body — its efferent pathways cross twice, effectively producing an ipsilateral net effect — rather than controlling muscles of the opposite (contralateral) side.

questions.learning_objective: State that the cerebellum's function is purely motor and operates at a subconscious level, distinguishing this from its specific lobar roles and its ipsilateral laterality.

questions.title: Craniofacial processes in unilateral cleft lip
questions.question: A 17-year-old girl uses Accutane, an acne drug implicated in interfering with normal development of the facial primordia, early in her unexpected pregnancy. Examination of the newborn reveals the presence of unilateral cleft upper lip. In this case, the defect is related to failure of fusion of what craniofacial processes?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Failure of fusion between the maxillary process and the lateral nasal process instead produces an oblique facial cleft, not a cleft lip.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fusion of the medial and lateral nasal processes forms the nostril and nasal ala; its failure is not the cause of upper-lip clefting.
explanations.C: Correct. The upper lip forms from fusion of the two medial nasal processes in the midline (forming the intermaxillary segment and philtrum) with the maxillary process on each side. Failure of fusion between a maxillary process and the medial nasal process on one side leaves a persistent gap lateral to the philtrum — a unilateral cleft lip, the most common form of cleft lip — and Accutane (isotretinoin), a known teratogen, is a recognized cause of such craniofacial malformations when taken in early pregnancy. In short: identify failure of maxillary-medial nasal process fusion as the mechanism of unilateral cleft lip.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Failure of the two medial nasal (intermaxillary) processes, or of the two maxillary processes, to fuse in the midline produces a median cleft lip, not the unilateral cleft described in this vignette.

questions.learning_objective: Identify failure of fusion between the maxillary process and medial nasal process as the cause of unilateral cleft lip, distinguishing it from median cleft lip and oblique facial cleft mechanisms.

questions.title: Location of spinal efferent motor neurons
questions.question: Where are efferent neurons of the motor system located in the spinal cord?

options.A: Dorsal white column of the spinal cord.
options.B: Ventral & lateral white column of spinal cord
options.C: Ventral & lateral horns of spinal cord

explanations.A: Incorrect. The dorsal white column is ascending white matter (axon tracts), not a location for neuronal cell bodies.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ventral and lateral white columns are likewise white matter (tracts of axons), not the grey-matter location of motor neuron cell bodies.
explanations.C: Correct. Alpha and gamma motor neurons (the efferent, lower motor neurons supplying skeletal muscle) have their cell bodies in the ventral (anterior) grey horn, while autonomic (sympathetic) preganglionic efferent neurons are located in the lateral grey horn at thoracolumbar levels — together, the ventral and lateral grey horns house the spinal cord's efferent neuron cell bodies. In short: identify the ventral and lateral grey horns, not any white column or the dorsal horn, as the location of the spinal cord's efferent (motor) neurons.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The dorsal (posterior) grey horn contains second-order sensory neuron cell bodies receiving incoming afferent input, not motor efferents.

questions.learning_objective: State that efferent (motor) neurons of the spinal cord are located in the ventral and lateral grey horns, not in white matter columns or the dorsal horn.

questions.title: Origin of the supraorbital artery
questions.question: The supraorbital artery is a branch from ONE of the following:

explanations.A: Correct. The supraorbital artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery (itself a branch of the internal carotid artery), emerging from the orbit through the supraorbital notch or foramen to supply the forehead and scalp, alongside its companion the supratrochlear artery. In short: identify the ophthalmic artery, not the subclavian, external carotid, or supratrochlear artery, as the parent vessel of the supraorbital artery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The first part of the subclavian artery gives rise to the vertebral artery, internal thoracic artery and thyrocervical trunk, none of which directly supplies the orbit.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The external carotid artery supplies the face via its facial, superficial temporal and maxillary branches, but not the supraorbital territory.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The supratrochlear artery is a sibling terminal branch of the ophthalmic artery, not the parent vessel of the supraorbital artery.

questions.learning_objective: State that the supraorbital artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery.

questions.title: Hypothalamic lesion causing anorexia
questions.question: Which hypothalamic lesion leads to Anorexia :

options.A: Destruction of the ventromedial group of nuclei
options.B: Stimulation of the lateral group of nuclei
options.C: Destruction of the lateral group of nuclei
options.D: Stimulation of the posterior group of nuclei

explanations.A: Incorrect. The ventromedial nucleus is the hypothalamic "satiety center"; its destruction instead causes hyperphagia and obesity, the opposite of anorexia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Stimulation, rather than destruction, of the lateral hypothalamic ("feeding center") nuclei would increase feeding behavior, again the opposite of anorexia.
explanations.C: Correct. The lateral hypothalamic nuclei constitute the "feeding" or "hunger center"; their destruction abolishes the desire to eat, producing anorexia and severe weight loss, while their stimulation instead induces feeding. In short: identify destruction of the lateral hypothalamic nuclei, not the ventromedial nucleus or stimulation of either group, as the lesion causing anorexia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Stimulation of the posterior hypothalamic group relates chiefly to sympathetic activation and thermoregulatory responses, not to feeding behavior.

questions.learning_objective: State that destruction of the lateral hypothalamic nuclei (the feeding center) causes anorexia, contrasting this with the ventromedial nucleus's opposite (satiety) role.

questions.title: Vertebral artery's point of entry into the skull
questions.question: The vertebral artery enters the skull through the following foramen:

explanations.A: Correct. Each vertebral artery ascends through the foramina transversaria of the upper cervical vertebrae, winds around the lateral mass of the atlas within the suboccipital triangle, pierces the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane and dura, and enters the cranial cavity through the foramen magnum, where the two vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery. In short: identify the foramen magnum, not the jugular foramen, internal auditory meatus or anterior condylar canal, as the vertebral artery's point of entry into the skull.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The jugular foramen transmits the internal jugular vein and cranial nerves IX, X and XI, not the vertebral artery.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The internal auditory meatus transmits cranial nerves VII and VIII along with the labyrinthine artery, not the vertebral artery.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The anterior condylar (hypoglossal) canal transmits cranial nerve XII, not the vertebral artery.

questions.subtopic: Entry into the skull via foramen magnum
questions.learning_objective: State that the vertebral artery enters the skull through the foramen magnum.

questions.title: Exception among the sequelae of parkinsonian rigidity
questions.question: In Parkinsonism all are sequelae of rigidity EXCEPT:

options.D: Loss of swinging of arms during walking

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception. Inability to move around freely (akinesia/bradykinesia) is a direct consequence of the sustained increase in muscle tone that is rigidity.
explanations.B: Correct as the exception. Pill-rolling tremor is a separate cardinal feature of Parkinson disease, arising from an oscillating basal ganglia circuit at rest, not a consequence of rigidity itself. In short: identify pill-rolling tremor, unlike the other listed features, as a distinct feature rather than a sequela of rigidity.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the exception. Mask facies (rigid, expressionless facial musculature) is a direct sequela of increased tone in the facial muscles.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the exception. Loss of the normal arm swing during gait results directly from sustained rigidity restricting the freedom of limb movement.

questions.subtopic: Sequelae of rigidity versus tremor as a separate feature
questions.learning_objective: Identify pill-rolling tremor as a separate cardinal feature of Parkinson disease, distinct from the sequelae directly produced by rigidity (bradykinesia, mask face, loss of arm swing).

questions.title: Basal ganglia circuit underlying cognitive function
questions.question: The cognitive function of basal ganglia is related to its connection with:

options.D: vital centers in the reticular formation

explanations.A: Incorrect. The vestibulocerebellum relates to balance and eye-movement control, not to basal ganglia cognitive circuitry.
explanations.B: Correct. The associative (cognitive) basal ganglia circuit runs chiefly through the caudate nucleus, which receives projections from, and returns output via the thalamus to, the prefrontal cortex, underlying executive function and the cognitive aspects of basal ganglia activity — distinct from the motor circuit (centered on the putamen) and the limbic circuit (centered on the ventral striatum). In short: identify the prefrontal cortex, not the vestibulocerebellum, suprachiasmatic nucleus or reticular formation, as the structure whose connection with the basal ganglia underlies their cognitive function.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The suprachiasmatic nucleus governs circadian rhythm, unrelated to basal ganglia cognitive circuitry.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vital centers of the reticular formation govern cardiovascular and respiratory reflexes, not cognitive basal ganglia loops.

questions.subtopic: Associative (cognitive) circuit and the prefrontal cortex
questions.learning_objective: State that the cognitive function of the basal ganglia is related to its connection with the prefrontal cortex, via the associative (caudate-based) circuit.

questions.title: Exception among vagus nerve branches
questions.question: Which of the following IS NOT a branch of the vagus nerve?

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception. The auricular branch (Arnold's nerve) of the vagus nerve is a genuine branch, supplying the external auditory meatus and concha.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the exception. The pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve genuinely joins the pharyngeal plexus.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the exception. The meningeal (recurrent) branch of the vagus nerve genuinely supplies the dura of the posterior cranial fossa.
explanations.D: Correct as the exception. The tympanic branch belongs instead to the glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX), known as Jacobson's nerve, which supplies the tympanic plexus of the middle ear — it is not a branch of the vagus nerve. In short: identify the tympanic branch, unlike the auricular, pharyngeal and meningeal branches, as belonging to the glossopharyngeal rather than the vagus nerve.

questions.subtopic: Vagus nerve branches (tympanic belongs to CN IX)
questions.learning_objective: Identify the tympanic branch as belonging to the glossopharyngeal nerve, not the vagus nerve, distinguishing it from the vagus's genuine auricular, pharyngeal and meningeal branches.

questions.title: Features of Betz cells
questions.question: Betz cells are:

options.A: Found in the inner pyramidal layer
options.C: They are prominent in the postcentral gyrus

explanations.A: Correct. Betz cells are giant pyramidal neurons located in layer V (the internal/inner pyramidal layer) of the primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus, and their large-diameter, heavily myelinated axons contribute to the corticospinal (pyramidal) tract. In short: identify the inner pyramidal layer as the location of Betz cells, not the postcentral gyrus, and recognize them as large (not small) upper (not lower) motor neurons.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Betz cells are among the largest neurons in the central nervous system, not small-sized.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Betz cells are found in the precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex), not the postcentral gyrus, which is somatosensory cortex.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Betz cells are upper motor neurons, originating fibers of the corticospinal tract, not lower motor neurons (which are located in the spinal cord and brainstem).

questions.learning_objective: State that Betz cells are giant upper motor neurons found in the inner pyramidal layer (layer V) of the precentral gyrus.

questions.title: Functional property of the fovea centralis
questions.question: The fovea centralis of the retina:

options.A: is the region of the highest visual acuity

explanations.A: Correct. The fovea centralis, at the center of the macula, is densely packed exclusively with cone photoreceptors and has minimal neural convergence (close to a 1:1 cone-to-ganglion-cell ratio), giving it the sharpest spatial resolution and the highest visual acuity anywhere in the retina, used for detailed central vision. In short: identify the fovea centralis as the region of highest visual acuity, not the lowest light threshold, rod-only composition or scotopic specialization.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The fovea has the highest light threshold (is the least sensitive to dim light) among retinal regions, since cones require brighter light than rods to respond — the opposite of the lowest threshold.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The fovea contains only cones, not rods.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The fovea is specialized for photopic (bright-light, color, high-acuity) vision, not scotopic (dim-light, rod-mediated) vision.

questions.learning_objective: State that the fovea centralis is the region of highest visual acuity in the retina, being cone-only and specialized for photopic (not scotopic) vision.

questions.title: Classification of the cingulum
questions.question: Cingulum is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Ascending fibers" is not a standard classification category for cerebral white matter tracts, which are classified as association, commissural or projection fibers.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Commissural fibers cross the midline to connect the two cerebral hemispheres (e.g. the corpus callosum), which the cingulum, an intrahemispheric tract, does not do.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Projection fibers connect the cortex with subcortical structures or the spinal cord (e.g. the corticospinal and thalamocortical tracts), unlike the cingulum's purely intrahemispheric course.
explanations.D: Correct. The cingulum is a long association fiber bundle running within the cingulate gyrus and continuing into the parahippocampal gyrus, interconnecting frontal, parietal and temporal regions of the same hemisphere as part of the limbic system's white matter — the defining feature of an association tract. In short: identify the cingulum as an association fiber tract, not a commissural or projection tract.

questions.learning_objective: Classify the cingulum as an association fiber tract, connecting regions within the same cerebral hemisphere.

questions.title: Exception among effects of semicircular canal stimulation
questions.question: All result from semicircular canals stimulation EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception. Nystagmus, a reflex eye movement via the vestibulo-ocular reflex, is a classic effect of semicircular canal stimulation.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the exception. Vertigo, an illusory sense of rotation, is a classic effect of semicircular canal stimulation.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the exception. Vomiting, via vestibular connections to the brainstem vomiting center, is a recognized effect of semicircular canal stimulation.
explanations.D: Correct as the exception. Contralateral extensor hypertonia is instead associated with static (otolith/utricular) labyrinthine reflexes that regulate postural tone via the vestibulospinal tract, not with a direct effect of semicircular canal (rotational, dynamic) stimulation. In short: identify contralateral extensor hypertonia, unlike nystagmus, vertigo and vomiting, as not a direct result of semicircular canal stimulation.

questions.learning_objective: Identify contralateral extensor hypertonia as not a direct effect of semicircular canal stimulation, distinguishing it from nystagmus, vertigo and vomiting.

questions.title: Functional role of the amygdala in the limbic system
questions.question: The amygdala in the limbic system is concerned with:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Facilitation of muscle tone is a function of brainstem reticular, cerebellar and basal ganglia circuits, not the amygdala.
explanations.B: Correct. The amygdala, a key limbic system nucleus in the medial temporal lobe, attaches emotional significance (especially fear) to experiences and modulates the strength and consolidation of memories for emotionally-charged events, working closely with the hippocampus in this process. In short: identify consolidation of emotional memories as the amygdala's role, not muscle tone facilitation, movement prediction, or temperature regulation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Prediction of movements relates chiefly to cerebellar (and to some extent premotor cortical) circuitry, not the amygdala.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Body temperature regulation is a hypothalamic, not amygdalar, function.

questions.learning_objective: State that the amygdala is concerned with the consolidation of emotional memories, distinguishing this from hypothalamic, cerebellar and brainstem functions.

questions.title: Afferent input to the reticular formation
questions.question: Reticular formation receives impulses from:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The inferior colliculus is itself a relay station further along the auditory pathway, downstream of the cochlear nuclei, rather than the direct source of the collateral input credited here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The medial geniculate body is a thalamic auditory relay further downstream still, not the direct source of the collateral input to the reticular formation being tested.
explanations.C: Correct. The reticular formation receives collateral input from ascending sensory pathways as they pass through the brainstem, including auditory collaterals branching directly from the cochlear nuclei, contributing to the reticular formation's role in maintaining generalized cortical arousal via the ascending reticular activating system. In short: identify the cochlear nuclei, among these choices, as a source of afferent input to the reticular formation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The inferior olivary nuclei chiefly supply climbing fibers to the cerebellum, and are not the cochlear-pathway source of reticular formation input being tested here.

questions.learning_objective: State that the reticular formation receives collateral afferent input from the cochlear nuclei, among the ascending sensory pathways passing through the brainstem.

questions.title: Kinocilium orientation in the horizontal semicircular canal
questions.question: Crista ampularis, In the horizontal semicircular canal (SCC) :

options.C: Depolarizes with the stereocilia deviated away from the kinocilium

explanations.A: Incorrect. Each hair cell has multiple stereocilia, graded in height, not a single stereocilium.
explanations.B: Correct. In the horizontal (lateral) semicircular canal, each hair cell's single kinocilium is positioned on the utricular side of the stereocilia bundle, so that endolymph flow deflecting the stereocilia toward the kinocilium (utriculopetal flow) depolarizes the cell — the opposite polarity arrangement from the vertical (superior and posterior) canals, where the kinocilium lies away from the utricle. In short: identify that in the horizontal canal, the kinocilium lies toward the utricle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Deviation of the stereocilia away from (not toward) the kinocilium hyperpolarizes (inhibits), rather than depolarizes, the hair cell.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Each hair cell has a single kinocilium, not multiple.

questions.learning_objective: State that in the horizontal semicircular canal, the kinocilium of each crista ampullaris hair cell lies toward the utricle, so that utriculopetal endolymph flow is depolarizing.

questions.title: Exception among eyelid structural components
questions.question: The eyelid contains all the following. Except:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception. The tarsal plate, a dense connective tissue skeleton, is a genuine structural component of the eyelid.
explanations.B: Correct as the exception. Zonular fibers (the suspensory ligament of the lens, running from the ciliary body to the lens equator) belong to the lens and ciliary apparatus deep within the globe, not to the eyelid. In short: identify zonular fibers, unlike the tarsal plate, smooth muscle and blood vessels, as not a component of the eyelid.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the exception. Smooth muscle (such as the superior and inferior tarsal muscles of Müller) is a genuine structural component of the eyelid.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the exception. A rich blood supply is a genuine structural feature of the eyelid.

questions.learning_objective: Identify zonular fibers as belonging to the lens/ciliary apparatus, not the eyelid, distinguishing them from genuine eyelid components (tarsal plate, smooth muscle, blood vessels).

questions.title: Ventricular derivative of the hindbrain cavity
questions.question: Which of the following spaces is formed from the cavity of the hindbrain?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The central canal of the spinal cord derives from the caudal (spinal cord) portion of the neural tube, not the hindbrain.
explanations.B: Correct. During neural tube development, the central cavity of the rhombencephalon (hindbrain) expands into the fourth ventricle, situated between the pons and medulla ventrally and the cerebellum dorsally. In short: identify the fourth ventricle, not the central canal, lateral ventricles or third ventricle, as the derivative of the hindbrain cavity.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lateral ventricles derive from the telencephalic vesicles (cerebral hemispheres), not the hindbrain.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The third ventricle derives from the diencephalon, not the hindbrain.

questions.subtopic: Fourth ventricle as a hindbrain-cavity derivative
questions.learning_objective: State that the fourth ventricle is the derivative of the hindbrain's central cavity, distinguishing it from the lateral ventricles, third ventricle and central canal.

questions.title: Zonal location of hypothalamic nuclei
questions.question: The following statement regarding hypothalamic nuclei is true:

options.A: Supraoptic nucleus is in the mammillary zone
options.B: Medail mammillary nucleus is in the posterior zone
options.C: Preoptic nucleus is in the lateral zone.
options.D: Paraventricular nucleus is in the intermediate zone

explanations.A: Incorrect. The supraoptic nucleus lies in the anterior (supraoptic) zone, not the mammillary (posterior) zone.
explanations.B: Correct. The hypothalamus is classically divided, from front to back, into supraoptic (anterior), tuberal (middle/intermediate) and mammillary (posterior) zones; the medial mammillary nucleus, part of the mammillary body complex, sits within this posterior (mammillary) zone. In short: identify the medial mammillary nucleus as located in the posterior zone of the hypothalamus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The preoptic nucleus lies in the most anterior (preoptic) region, not the lateral zone, which is a medial-lateral rather than anteroposterior subdivision.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The paraventricular nucleus lies in the anterior (supraoptic) zone, not the intermediate (tuberal) zone.

questions.subtopic: Anteroposterior zonal organization of hypothalamic nuclei
questions.learning_objective: State that the medial mammillary nucleus lies in the posterior (mammillary) zone of the hypothalamus, per its anteroposterior zonal organization.

questions.title: Exception among chorda tympani nerve statements
questions.question: Regarding the chorda tympani nerve, the following are correct EXCEPT:

options.A: It is a branch of facial nerve inside the middle ear cavity
options.B: t carries general and taste sensations from anterior 2/3 of tongue
options.C: it carries secretomotor fibers to the submandibular gland
options.D: it carries secretomotor fibers to the sublingual gland

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception. The chorda tympani genuinely branches from the facial nerve and traverses the middle ear cavity, medial to the tympanic membrane.
explanations.B: Correct as the exception. The chorda tympani carries taste sensation only from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue; general (tactile) sensation there is instead carried separately by the lingual nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve — the chorda tympani does not carry general sensation. In short: identify the chorda tympani as carrying taste only, not general sensation, from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the exception. The chorda tympani genuinely carries preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers, via the submandibular ganglion, to the submandibular gland.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the exception. The chorda tympani genuinely carries preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers, via the submandibular ganglion, to the sublingual gland.

questions.subtopic: Chorda tympani function (taste only, not general sensation)
questions.learning_objective: Identify that the chorda tympani carries taste, not general sensation, from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, while correctly carrying secretomotor fibers to the submandibular and sublingual glands.

questions.title: Brain fuel source in the fed state
questions.question: During fed state brain can get energy from:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ketone bodies become a significant brain fuel only in the fasting/starved state, once hepatic fatty-acid oxidation produces them in quantity, not in the fed state.
explanations.B: Correct. In the fed (well-nourished, non-fasting) state, the brain relies almost exclusively on glucose as its energy substrate, since glucose crosses the blood-brain barrier efficiently via GLUT transporters while neurons have very limited capacity to oxidize fatty acids. In short: identify glucose as the brain's energy source in the fed state.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lactate can serve as an alternative fuel in specific contexts (such as intense exercise or the neonatal period), but it is not the fed-state brain's primary or default fuel — glucose is.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fatty acids cannot cross the blood-brain barrier in physiologically significant amounts and are not used by neurons as an energy source.

questions.learning_objective: State that in the fed state, the brain's energy source is glucose, contrasting this with the fasting state's reliance on ketone bodies.

questions.title: Exception among the basal ganglia nuclei
questions.question: Basal ganglia include all the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception. The subthalamic nucleus is a genuine component of the basal ganglia.
explanations.B: Correct as the exception. The dentate nucleus is instead the largest and most lateral of the deep cerebellar nuclei, unrelated to the basal ganglia despite the superficial similarity in naming to other extrapyramidal-system nuclei. In short: identify the dentate nucleus, unlike the subthalamic nucleus, caudate nucleus and substantia nigra, as a cerebellar rather than basal ganglia structure.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the exception. The caudate nucleus is a genuine component of the basal ganglia.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the exception. The substantia nigra is a genuine component of the basal ganglia.

questions.subtopic: Dentate nucleus excluded (cerebellar, not basal ganglia)
questions.learning_objective: Identify the dentate nucleus as a deep cerebellar nucleus, not a basal ganglia structure, distinguishing it from the subthalamic nucleus, caudate nucleus and substantia nigra.

questions.title: Course of the anterior cerebral artery
questions.question: The anterior cerebral artery lies in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The central sulcus, on the lateral/superomedial surface, is not accompanied by the main trunk of the anterior cerebral artery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lateral (Sylvian) sulcus houses the middle cerebral artery, not the anterior cerebral artery.
explanations.C: Correct. After curving around the genu of the corpus callosum, the anterior cerebral artery continues posteriorly as the pericallosal artery within the callosal sulcus, immediately above the corpus callosum, supplying the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes along its course. In short: identify the callosal sulcus as the course of the anterior cerebral artery.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The posterior calcarine sulcus, in the occipital lobe, is supplied by branches of the posterior cerebral artery, not the anterior cerebral artery.

questions.subtopic: Anterior cerebral artery course in the callosal sulcus
questions.learning_objective: State that the anterior cerebral artery (as the pericallosal artery) courses within the callosal sulcus.

questions.title: Relation of the caudate body to the lateral ventricle
questions.question: Body of caudate is related to which part of lateral ventricle:

explanations.A: Correct. The C-shaped caudate nucleus follows the curve of the lateral ventricle: its head bulges into the anterior (frontal) horn, its body runs along the floor of the central part (body) of the lateral ventricle, and its tail curves through the roof of the inferior (temporal) horn down to the amygdala. In short: identify the central part of the lateral ventricle as related to the body of the caudate nucleus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The posterior (occipital) horn is related instead to the tapetum and optic radiation fibers, not the caudate body.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The anterior horn is related to the caudate head, not its body.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The inferior horn is related to the caudate tail, not its body.

questions.subtopic: Caudate body and the central part of the lateral ventricle
questions.learning_objective: State that the body of the caudate nucleus is related to the central part of the lateral ventricle, distinguishing this from the head (anterior horn) and tail (inferior horn) relations.

questions.title: Muscle forming the floor of the carotid triangle
questions.question: The following muscle shares in forming the floor of the carotid triangle:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The superior belly of omohyoid forms one of the carotid triangle's boundaries, not its floor.
explanations.B: Correct. The floor of the carotid triangle is formed by parts of three muscles — the thyrohyoid, the hyoglossus, and the middle constrictor of the pharynx — while the triangle's boundaries are formed by the digastric, the superior belly of omohyoid (or stylohyoid) and sternocleidomastoid. In short: identify the middle constrictor of the pharynx as one of the muscles forming the carotid triangle's floor.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sternothyroid is a strap muscle of the anterior (muscular) triangle, deep to sternohyoid, and is not involved in forming the carotid triangle's floor.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mylohyoid forms the floor of the submental/submandibular region (oral cavity floor), not the carotid triangle.

questions.learning_objective: State that the middle constrictor of the pharynx is one of the muscles forming the floor of the carotid triangle.

questions.title: Effect of post-tetanic stimulation on synaptic transmission
questions.question: A post tetanic stimulation of a synaptic neurons for a short time causes:

options.B: Opening of the voltage gated Ca++ channels in the post synaptic membrane
options.C: Delayed opening of the voltage gated K+ channels.
options.D: Increase in their neurotransmitter release and synaptic potentiation

explanations.A: Incorrect. Synaptic fatigue is the opposite phenomenon — a decline in transmission with prolonged or repeated stimulation, from transmitter depletion — not what follows a brief tetanic stimulus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels central to this process are located on the presynaptic terminal, not the postsynaptic membrane.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The defining mechanism of post-tetanic potentiation is presynaptic residual calcium accumulation, not a delayed postsynaptic potassium channel event.
explanations.D: Correct. Brief high-frequency (tetanic) presynaptic stimulation causes residual calcium to accumulate within the presynaptic terminal faster than it can be cleared, so that a subsequent test stimulus triggers exaggerated neurotransmitter release. This phenomenon, post-tetanic potentiation, produces a transiently enhanced (facilitated) postsynaptic response and is considered a simple cellular model of short-term synaptic plasticity. In short: identify increased neurotransmitter release and synaptic potentiation as the effect of brief post-tetanic stimulation.

questions.learning_objective: State that brief post-tetanic stimulation causes increased neurotransmitter release and synaptic potentiation, via presynaptic residual calcium accumulation.

questions.title: Exception among the cortical language centers
questions.question: Language centers include all the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Correct as the exception. The general somatosensory association areas 5 and 7 (superior parietal lobule) process and integrate somatosensory information, not language, so they are not part of the cortical language network. In short: identify sensory association areas 5 and 7, unlike area 39, Broca's area and Wernicke's area, as not part of the cortical language system.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the exception. Area 39 (the angular gyrus) is a genuine component of the cortical language network, involved in reading and cross-modal association linking visual word forms to their auditory/semantic representations.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the exception. Broca's area (areas 44/45) is a genuine, well-established component of the cortical language network, responsible for expressive/motor speech.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the exception. Wernicke's area is a genuine, well-established component of the cortical language network, responsible for language comprehension.

questions.subtopic: Cortical language centers (somatosensory association areas excluded)
questions.learning_objective: Identify the somatosensory association areas 5 and 7 as not part of the cortical language network, distinguishing them from Broca's area, Wernicke's area and area 39.
